No Fixed Address

There's no bell-cow to bank on — the lead back sees just 50% of carries (league ~59%), a committee that caps any one back's ceiling and makes their rushing props matchup- and script-dependent.

The Offensive Blueprint

In the passing game the ball funnels to Malik Nabers — 29% of targets (league ~23%), a genuine alpha share that concentrates the receiving value at the top.

They run downhill — mostly inside the tackles (18% to the edge vs ~25%), a gap/power scheme that trades big plays for a steady, grinding floor.

The WR2 is unusually involved here — 19% of targets (league ~15%), meaning there's bankable volume beyond the top receiver.

They lean on tempo — a 17% no-huddle rate (league ~11%) that inflates snap counts and everyone's volume.

The tight end is barely used in the passing game (11% of targets vs ~15%) — fade their TE's receiving props.

By the numbers it's a struggling unit — a 41% success rate (below the 44% average).

In the Red Zone

Inside the 20 they lean run-heavy, passing 50% of the time, funnelling touchdown equity to Tyrone Tracy Jr..

Defense — The Run Comes Free

They surrender 142 rushing and 229 passing yards per game (league ~120 / ~230). The run moves against them — target opposing RB1s.

They lock down opposing tight ends — just 26 rec yds/game (vs ~35); fade receiving props there.

They lock down opposing WR1s — just 53 rec yds/game (vs ~58); fade receiving props there.

They lock down opposing WR2s — just 32 rec yds/game (vs ~36); fade receiving props there.

They leak RB rushing TDs (0.53/game vs ~0.46) — an anytime-TD spot to attack.

Broadly a leaky unit — 46% success rate allowed (vs ~44%); points come easy against them.

The Betting Angles

Bottom line: opposing RB1s smash on the ground and at the goal line.

Built on 2024–25 data; the profile rebuilds through the season as the current staff and roster set their own tendencies.
